hints: Look closely at the table. Plant X takes up about 16.9 mm3 by 10 minutes while Y takes up only 4.9 mm3, but what is different about the two shoots themselves that was never measured?
Remember a potometer measures total water uptake for the whole shoot. Think about how you would fairly compare transpiration between a big leafy shoot and a small shoot.
walkthrough:
**Observe what the data really show**

Look at the table. At every time, X has taken up much more water than Y.

By 10 minutes, X is at $16.9 \ mm^3$ and Y is at only $4.9 \ mm^3$. The student assumes this means Y loses less water because it is a xerophyte.

**Recall what a potometer measures**

A potometer measures water uptake by the whole shoot, which is assumed to equal water lost by transpiration.

Total uptake depends on transpiration rate AND on how much leaf surface is transpiring:
$$total \ uptake = rate \ per \ unit \ area \times leaf \ area \times time$$

**Spot the uncontrolled variable**

The question tells us time, room and potometers were the same. That controls the environment.

But it tells us nothing about the size of the two shoots. If Y simply had fewer or smaller leaves, its total uptake would be lower even if it was not a xerophyte. To conclude about adaptation, we must compare uptake per $mm^2$ of leaf, not total $mm^3$.

options.A: Both plants were tested at the same time in the same room, so air flow and temperature were already the same for X and Y.
options.B: Both plants were set up together, so any lack of acclimatisation would affect both similarly and cannot explain the large consistent difference.
options.C: At 0 minutes uptake is zero by definition, so missing this reading does not affect the comparison of the trends from 2 to 10 minutes.
options.D: Leaf area was not standardised. A smaller total leaf area in Y would give lower total uptake, so we cannot conclude Y has a lower transpiration rate or is a xerophyte.
